props.title: Three Coins in the Fountain
props.initialSlug: Three women seek love and destiny in Rome

sections.content: Three Coins in the Fountain (1954) established the romantic template for American films set in Rome, capturing the city's postwar allure when international travel was still a luxury for most viewers. Shot in stunning CinemaScope, it popularized the Trevi Fountain as a must-see landmark and inspired countless tourists to toss coins while making wishes. The film's influence echoes through later Rome-set romances like Roman Holiday (1953) and La Dolce Vita (1960), establishing the Eternal City as cinema's ultimate backdrop for finding love abroad.

sections.content: The film's success sparked Hollywood's love affair with international location shooting. To Catch a Thief (1955) showcased the French Riviera, while Summertime (1955) turned Venice into a character itself. These productions marked a shift from studio backlots to authentic European locations, giving American audiences their first vivid glimpses of postwar Europe's recovery and glamour.

Jean Negulesco's direction in Three Coins in the Fountain pioneered techniques for shooting in CinemaScope, particularly in capturing architecture and cityscapes. His work influenced later films like An American in Paris (1951) and Funny Face (1957), which similarly used widescreen photography to showcase European locations as integral elements of their romantic narratives. SUBHEAD: The American Abroad Romance Genre

movies.title: Summertime
movies.slug: Katharine Hepburn plays a lonely American tourist who finds unexpected romance in Venice.

sections.content: The film established key tropes of the Americans-abroad romance genre: culture clash, career versus love choices, and the transformative power of European settings. These themes would be revisited in films like Light in the Piazza (1962) and later in modern interpretations like Under the Tuscan Sun (2003) and Letters to Juliet (2010), all sharing DNA with Three Coins' original formula.
